newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan pork crisis generates island-wide jitters.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan pork crisis generates island-wide jitters.

text.p: Aside from serious economic distress, Taiwan's hog epidemic has also bred social anxiety, with piglet-slaughtering soldiers suffering nightmares and suspicions raised that rival China planted the deadly disease.

Scrambling to calm public fears six days into an island-wide outbreak of hog foot and mouth disease, the government ruling Nationalist Party on Wednesday urged all officials to eat more pork and to serve pork dishes at banquets.
"If an official is using taxpayers' money, the meal he eats has to include at least two pork dishes," Nationalist lawmaker and spokesman Hung Shing-jung announced.
Some restaurants have stopped serving pork altogether and many consumers have simply stopped buying a meat that in normal times is easily the favourite among Taiwan's ethnic Chinese.
These are not normal times.
Nearly 400,000 hogs, even healthy ones, have died or been slaughtered in an army-led eradication campaign to prevent further spreading of the highly contagious virus.
Officials say the kill count could reach 15 percent of the island's 11 million pigs, or 1.6 million animals.

Across the island, masked soldiers in plastic suits have wielded electric prods to stun pigs, then used huge earth movers to dump them into incinerators or giant pits -- often with the pigs still gasping for air.

Some of the soldiers -- almost all of them mandatory conscripts under 25 years old -- became so distraught over their life-terminating duties that they have suffered recurring nightmares, forcing the army to grant extended leaves.
"Some of my brothers (fellow soldiers) had nightmares and were talking scary stuff in their dreams," said one soldier assigned to the extermination detail.
"One brother was so shaken that he was given a three-day holiday," he added.
Amid heated debates on how the deadly disease sprouted, one popular enemy was mentioned frequently as the guilty party -- communist China.
"We must be careful, because it is possible this whole thing came from the mainland," a man told one of the endless call-in radio shows about the epidemic. "We shouldn't be too naive."
Provincial lawmaker Hsu Teng-kung alleged that the disease was "definitely the work of communist bandit spies" trying to bring Taiwan under Beijing's control.
Taiwan and China have been rivals since a bitter civil war ended in 1949, and Beijing's communist government still vows to retake the island, by force if necessary.

Since the outbreak was confirmed on March 20, investigators have said the virus probably came from China's southern Hainan island -- an unwelcome side-effect of rampant pork smuggling across the Taiwan strait.
The pork-eating public was exercising great caution.
In Taipei's Nada Japanese restaurant, a customer warily asked the chef whether he had been served pork instead of the lamb he had ordered.
"We are no longer serving pork. There is simply no demand for it," the chef responded.
While people were shunning hogs and pork, animals in the Taipei zoo have been forced by their keepers to avoid contact with the most likely carriers of the virus -- people.
"We are not protecting the people from the animals. Rather, we are protecting the animals from the people," a Taipei Zoo spokesman said by telephone.
